name: Niger River
summary: West Africa's principal river; enters Nigeria from Niger Republic and flows south to the Niger Delta.
description: The Niger is the third-longest river in Africa. Inside Nigeria it passes through the northwest, the Middle Belt confluence at Lokoja, and fans into the world's third-largest delta. It supports hydropower (Kainji, Jebba, Shiroro on tributaries), inland navigation, and the oil-bearing delta wetlands.
lengthNote: About 1,300 km of the course lies in Nigeria
sourceNote: Guinea Highlands (outside Nigeria); enters Nigeria near the Niger Republic border in Kebbi
mouthNote: Gulf of Guinea via the Niger Delta (Nun, Forcados and many creeks)
economy: Hydropower, inland waterways, fisheries, irrigation, and the delta petroleum basin.
ecology: Floodplain agriculture (fadama), manatee and fish diversity, mangrove delta.
significance: Kainji Dam, Lokoja confluence, Niger Delta outlet, historic trade corridor.

name: Benue River
summary: The Niger's largest tributary; enters from Cameroon and meets the Niger at Lokoja.
description: The Benue drains the Cameroon highlands and the Nigerian Middle Belt. Seasonal floods fertilise yam and rice plains in Adamawa, Taraba, and Benue. Makurdi is the main urban crossing. The confluence at Lokoja is one of West Africa's great geographic landmarks.
mouthNote: Joins the Niger at Lokoja, Kogi State
economy: Irrigation, fisheries, sand mining, and a historic (now limited) inland waterway.
ecology: Seasonal floodplains; hippo and fish habitats; erosion on sandy banks.
significance: Agricultural belt, Makurdi bridge, confluence at Lokoja.

name: Cross River
summary: Eastern river forming much of the Cameroon border before the Gulf of Guinea.
description: The Cross (Oyono) drains rainforest of Cross River State and western Cameroon. It is associated with Cross River National Park, Calabar port access, and high freshwater biodiversity. Seasonal floods affect Ogoja–Ikom–Calabar corridors.
mouthNote: Cross River estuary near Calabar, Gulf of Guinea
economy: Port access, fisheries, timber hinterland, border trade.
ecology: Rainforest, primates (including Cross River gorilla in the wider basin), estuary mangroves.
significance: Rainforest ecology, Calabar port, international border.

name: Kaduna River
summary: Major tributary of the Niger flowing through Kaduna and Niger states.
description: The Kaduna (named from 'crocodile' in Hausa, Kada) gives Kaduna city its name. It joins the Niger in Niger State. Shiroro Dam is a major hydro station on the system.
significance: Kaduna city namesake, Shiroro hydro, joins Niger.

name: Sokoto River
summary: Principal river of north-western Nigeria; feeds the Rima and Niger systems.
description: The Sokoto–Rima basin is the agricultural heart of the far northwest. Seasonal flooding supports irrigation schemes and grazing. The Bakolori and Goronyo dams regulate parts of the system.
mouthNote: Niger River via the Rima in Kebbi / Niger
economy: Irrigation (Bakolori, Goronyo), millet and rice, livestock.
significance: Sokoto basin irrigation, seasonal flooding, Hausa–Fulani heartland.

name: Gongola River
summary: Major Benue tributary draining the Bauchi–Gombe plateau and Adamawa foothills.
description: The Gongola flows through northeastern Nigeria before joining the Benue. Its basin supports rice, sorghum, and livestock in a savanna–Sahel transition zone. Seasonal floods shape farming calendars in Gombe and Adamawa.

name: Ogun River
summary: Southwestern river flowing through Ogun State toward the Lagos Lagoon.
description: The Ogun drains Yoruba highlands and feeds the Lagos Lagoon system with the Osun. It supports Abeokuta's water supply, quarrying, and peri-urban agriculture along its banks.
economy: Urban water, quarrying, agriculture, lagoon fisheries.
ecology: Forest–savanna transition; urban pollution pressure downstream.
significance: Abeokuta water source, Lagos Lagoon feeder.

name: Hadejia River
summary: Northeastern river feeding the Hadejia–Nguru wetlands and Komadugu Yobe system.
description: The Hadejia is central to one of Nigeria's largest seasonal wetland complexes. Flood recession farming and fishing depend on its pulse. Upstream dams and climate change have altered flow regimes.
ecology: Seasonal wetlands; bird habitat; drought sensitivity.

name: Komadugu Yobe
summary: Northeastern river system flowing toward Lake Chad via the Hadejia–Nguru wetlands.
description: The Komadugu Yobe (Yobe River) drains the Chad basin fringe of Nigeria. It connects to seasonal channels toward Lake Chad and supports transhumance corridors in Borno and Yobe.
economy: Pastoralism, recession farming, cross-border trade toward Chad.
ecology: Sahel channels; Lake Chad basin dependency.
significance: Lake Chad feeder system, Sahel livelihoods.

name: Imo River
summary: Major river of the southeast flowing through Imo toward Rivers State and the delta.
description: The Imo drains the rain-fed southeast and feeds delta creeks. It is important for oil-palm landscapes, local fisheries, and as a cultural boundary river among Igbo communities.
economy: Oil palm, fisheries, sand, local transport.
significance: Oil palm belt, local fisheries, delta tributary.

name: Osun River
summary: Sacred Yoruba river flowing through Osun State toward the Lagos lagoon system.
description: The Osun is central to Yoruba cosmology (Ọṣun). The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove on its banks is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Hydrologically it is part of the Ogun–Osun drainage toward the Lagos Lagoon.
economy: Water supply, tourism/festival economy, peri-urban agriculture.
ecology: Sacred grove forest remnant; urban pressure downstream.
significance: Osun-Osogbo heritage, Osogbo festival, Lagos water supply.

name: Anambra River
summary: Important Niger tributary draining Anambra and Enugu states into the main stem.
description: The Anambra (Omambala) is a key southeastern tributary of the Niger. Its floodplains support yam and rice farming and local fisheries. Onitsha sits at its confluence zone with the Niger.

name: Nun River
summary: Major Niger distributary carrying a large share of Niger flow to the Atlantic through Bayelsa.
description: The Nun is one of the Niger's primary delta outlets. It is lined with oil infrastructure, riverine settlements, and mangrove. Navigation and pipeline corridors follow its banks. Seasonal flooding shapes Ijaw livelihoods.
economy: Oil logistics, river transport, artisanal fishing.
ecology: Mangrove and freshwater swamp; oil-spill exposure.
significance: Main Niger outlet branch, oil corridor, Ijaw riverine heartland.

name: Forcados River
summary: Western delta channel serving historic Forcados oil terminal and navigation.
description: Forcados was a Royal Niger Company and later oil-export anchorage. The river remains a pipeline and terminal access route in Delta State, with mixed fishing and oil-service traffic.
economy: Crude export logistics, fishing, bunkering-risk waterway.
significance: Forcados oil terminal, pipeline hub, colonial-era ocean outlet.

name: Escravos River
summary: Delta channel serving Warri and the Escravos gas-to-liquids / terminal complex.
description: Escravos ('slaves' in Portuguese, a colonial toponym) is now synonymous with Chevron and gas infrastructure. The waterway links Warri's industrial waterfront to the Bight of Benin.
significance: Escravos GTL, Warri access, western delta energy corridor.

name: Bonny River
summary: Deep channel to Port Harcourt and Bonny Island LNG and oil terminals.
description: The Bonny estuary is Nigeria's premier LNG (NLNG) and a historic Ibani (Bonny) kingdom waterway. Large tankers and LNG carriers use dredged channels. Port Harcourt's port sits upriver.
economy: LNG, crude export, Port Harcourt harbour, oil services.
significance: NLNG Bonny Island, PH port, eastern export gateway.

name: New Calabar River
summary: Creek system west of Port Harcourt used for fisheries and peri-urban waterways.
description: The New Calabar (Kalabari) river system serves Kalabari communities and PH's western waterfront. It is important for artisanal fishing and local transport rather than deep-sea export.
